description:
We aim to explore how MODIS and VIIRS satellite data can be combined to better identify, analyze, and monitor fire hotspots. Our goal is to develop a practical solution that makes satellite data easier to understand and helps provide useful insights into fire detection and monitoring.

We are interested in using our skills in software development, data analysis, and technology to tackle this challenge. We believe in sharing ideas, and working together to turn our ideas into something meaningful.
summary:
FireSight is a web application that turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS hotspot records from five satellites (MODIS on Terra and Aqua; VIIRS on S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) into one consistent burning-activity history for Pakistan, from November 2000 to today.

Merging these sensors naively creates false trends: Pakistan’s combined record jumps 5.5× when VIIRS arrives in 2012, while MODIS alone changes just 1.13×. FireSight maps every detection onto a common 1 km equal-area grid, compares sensors in 8-day windows and calibrates each satellite onto one reference scale. Tested on years held out from training, MODIS bias falls from −74% to +1%, and the artificial 2012 jump from +385% to +6%.

The result is an interactive burning calendar for any province, district or drawn area, with a like-for-like comparison of recent days against the historical median, anomaly detection, recurring critical burning windows, uncertainty ranges, a fire map and CSV export.

This matters because emergency managers, foresters and scientists need to know whether today’s burning is truly unusual and when to prepare. FireSight gives them a tested, transparent answer built entirely on open NASA data.
details:
What FireSight does

FireSight is a web application that turns more than 25 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire records into one consistent, tested history of burning activity. It is built around an interactive burning calendar for Pakistan, from November 2000 to the latest available day.

NASA’s fire record comes from five satellites: MODIS on Terra and Aqua (1 km pixels), and VIIRS on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 (375 m pixels). Because they see the Earth differently, their records cannot be compared directly. Merging them naively creates false trends: Pakistan’s combined record jumps 5.5× when VIIRS arrives in 2012, while MODIS alone changes only 1.13×. FireSight removes these sensor effects so that patterns, trends and anomalies reflect real changes in burning, not changes in satellites.

How it works

Collect: 1.87 million MODIS and VIIRS detections from the NASA FIRMS archive and API. Every file is kept unchanged and checksummed.

Normalize: every sensor is mapped to one format, with UTC and local solar time. Each sensor keeps its own confidence scale.

Spatial aggregation: detections are placed on a common 1 km equal-area grid, and unique active cells are counted per satellite. This removes most of the pixel-size difference.

Temporal aggregation: satellites are compared in 8-day windows per province, which smooths out clouds and overpass gaps.

Calibrate and harmonize: using the years when satellites overlap, each one is mapped onto the VIIRS S-NPP reference scale. The model is chosen by cross-validation and tested on years it never saw. The record is then carried by one satellite at a time, so it never jumps.

Generate fire intelligence:

a 0–100 activity index;

the burning calendar;

robust seasonal anomalies;

recurring critical burning windows;

uncertainty ranges.

On held-out years, MODIS bias against VIIRS falls from −73.9% to +1.0%, and the artificial jump when VIIRS was added falls from +385% to +6%. Calibrated NOAA-21 agrees with S-NPP at a rank correlation of 0.98.

Benefits

Is this normal right now? One sentence compares the latest 7, 14 or 30 days with the same dates in every previous year.

When should we prepare? Critical windows show the weeks that burn in most years, for example 30 April – 20 May in at least 21 of 25 years in Pakistan.

Which events were truly unusual? Ranked anomaly episodes, such as the Sherani chilgoza pine-forest fire of May 2022.

Any area, any scale: the country, 7 provinces, 126 districts, a drawn polygon or a coordinate box. Includes a detection map, a CSV export of the harmonized series and the raw detections, and colour-blind-safe palettes.

Honest data quality: every value shows whether it was observed or reconstructed, its uncertainty, a reliability rating, and whether recent data are still provisional.

Intended impact

FireSight gives emergency managers, forest and land managers, and scientists a reliable baseline for fire activity. With it they can anticipate burning seasons, spot unusual conditions early, and target monitoring where it matters. In Pakistan this supports work on agricultural burning seasons and forest fires. Because it is built only on open NASA data and a documented, tested method, the same approach can be applied to other countries, as long as each region is calibrated with its own data. Areas outside Pakistan can already fetch recent raw FIRMS detections on demand.

Tools and technologies

Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1, VIIRS 375 m from S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21), the FIRMS missing-data table, geoBoundaries district and province boundaries, and NASA GIBS imagery.

Languages: Python 3.13 and TypeScript.

Data science: pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, pyproj, Shapely, SciPy and scikit-learn.

Storage and backend: Parquet files queried with DuckDB, served by a FastAPI REST API.

Frontend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS and Apache ECharts.

Quality and delivery: pytest (35 automated tests) and Git/GitHub.

Hardware: a standard laptop, with no GPU or cloud computing required.

What makes it creative

A calendar, not just a map: 25 years of daily satellite data compressed into one picture where burning seasons, unusual years and sensor-free trends are visible at a glance.

Harmonization you can see: a before-and-after view shows the naive merged record jumping while FireSight’s record stays consistent.

Like-for-like comparisons: “now” is always compared with the same calendar dates in every year, and checked again against years observed directly by VIIRS.

Fire stories: guided case studies on the live data turn statistics into narratives that anyone can follow.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty: we validate on held-out years, report all candidate models, and list our limitations in the app. VIIRS S-NPP is a reference scale, not ground truth. District estimates are less reliable than province or country ones. The calibration is fitted for Pakistan and is never applied elsewhere.

Data integrity: raw NASA files are never altered, and every result can be traced to its source file and row.

Responsible wording: a hotspot is a thermal anomaly, not a confirmed wildfire, and no detection does not mean no fire.

Accessibility: colour-vision-safe palettes and a layout that works on phones.

Security and reproducibility: API keys are never exposed, the data pipeline is documented, and package versions are pinned so anyone can rebuild the results.

Code and documentation: https://github.com/ubaid-create/firesight
